kcet|Chemistry|2026|28||0|0.s:
Balance the two half reactions, then combine.
Oxidation: C₂O₄²⁻ ⇒ 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ (each carbon goes +3 ⇒ +4, so 2 electrons per oxalate).
Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ ⇒ Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (Mn goes +7 ⇒ +2, so 5 electrons).
Electrons must cancel: LCM of 2 and 5 is 10, so take 5 oxalates and 2 permanganates.
5C₂O₄²⁻ ⇒ 10CO₂ + 10e⁻
2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10e⁻ ⇒ 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O
Adding: 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ ⇒ 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 10CO₂.
So a = 5, b = 2, c = 16, x = 2, y = 8, z = 10.
∴ a and x are 5 and 2.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|29||0|0:
An oxidising agent must be able to come down to a lower oxidation state.
All four species have the metal at +6, but chromium and molybdenum behave differently there.
Cr is a 3d metal: +6 is above its most stable state, so Cr(VI) drops readily to Cr(III).
That is why CrO₃, CrO₄²⁻ and Cr₂O₇²⁻ are all good oxidising agents.
Mo is a 4d metal, and down a group the higher oxidation state becomes more stable.
For molybdenum +6 is the stable state, so MoO₃ has little tendency to be reduced.
∴ MoO₃ will not act as an oxidising agent.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|30||0|0.s:
Fluorine is the more electronegative of the two, so on that ground alone you might expect it to
force the higher oxidation state — yet it does not. The reason is bonding capacity, not electronegativity.
Fluorine has no way to form a double bond: it uses its single unpaired electron and is then satisfied.
So each F can take only one of manganese's electrons, and MnF₄ uses up four.
Oxygen has two unpaired electrons and can form M=O double bonds.
Each oxygen therefore accounts for two of manganese's electrons, and in Mn₂O₇ this reaches +7.
∴ because in covalent compounds fluorine forms only single bonds while oxygen can form double bonds.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|31||0|0.s:
Write the configuration first. Cr has Z = 24: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹.
A cation loses the 4s electron before any 3d electron.
Cr²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁴ — remove the 4s¹ and one 3d electron.
Four electrons in five d orbitals stay unpaired by Hund's rule, so n = 4.
Spin-only moment: μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM
μ = √(4 × 6) = √24 = 4.899 BM.
∴ about 4.90 BM.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|32||0|0.s:
Compare the ligands, because the metal is iron in every case.
H₂O is a neutral monodentate ligand and a weak field one, so [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is the least stable here.
CO and CN⁻ are strong field monodentate ligands, giving genuinely stable complexes.
Oxalate, C₂O₄²⁻, is different in kind: it is bidentate, binding through both its oxygens.
Three oxalates therefore close three five-membered rings around the iron.
This is the chelate effect — releasing six water molecules to bind three ligands raises the entropy,
so ΔG is more negative and a ring complex is far harder to pull apart than the equivalent monodentate one.
∴ [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ is the most stable.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|33||0|0.s:
Only what lies outside the square brackets dissociates in solution.
The six NH₃ are inside the coordination sphere, bonded to cobalt, and stay with it.
The two chlorides are written outside, so they are ionisable.
[Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₂ ⇒ [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ + 2Cl⁻
Count them: one complex cation plus two chloride anions.
∴ 3 ions per molecule.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|34||0|0.s:
This describes synergic bonding in a metal carbonyl, and both halves of it are right.
Statement I — the carbon of CO carries a lone pair, and it donates that pair into an empty
d orbital on the metal. That is the M ← C σ bond.
Statement II — the metal now has excess electron density, so it pushes a filled d orbital's pair
back into the empty π* antibonding orbital of CO. That is the M → C π bond, called back-donation.
The two reinforce each other: σ donation makes the metal more electron rich, which drives more
back-donation, which in turn strengthens the σ bond. Hence 'synergic'.
Back-donation fills an antibonding orbital of CO, which is why the C–O bond lengthens and its
stretching frequency falls, exactly as observed.
∴ both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|40||0|0.s:
Use the two tests together.
Test 1 — salt + conc. H₂SO₄ gives a reddish brown gas.
Conc. H₂SO₄ oxidises bromide: 2Br⁻ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇒ Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O + SO₄²⁻.
Br₂ vapour is reddish brown. Chloride would give colourless HCl, iodide violet I₂ vapour,
and a carbonate would give colourless CO₂.
Test 2 — aqueous salt + AgNO₃ gives a pale yellow precipitate.
AgCl is white, AgBr is pale yellow and AgI is bright yellow; Ag₂CO₃ and Ag₂SO₄ are not pale yellow.
Both tests point the same way.
∴ the anion is Br⁻.
